newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. wants Angola troops longer, delays sanctions.
newsitem.headline: U.N. wants Angola troops longer, delays sanctions.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Friday said he wanted a delay in withdrawing U.N. troops from Angola and pointed the way toward sanctions against the rebel UNITA movement for flouting peace accords.

But while his written report said UNITA's latest last-minute "half-hearted concessions under pressure" were no longer acceptable, diplomats said U.N. officials nevertheless were checking them out before any sanctions were imposed.

"The United States supports additional sanctions," State Department spokesman James Rubin told reporters in Washington. "However, we're prepared to give the (U.N.) secretary-general flexibility if he thinks he needs it ...
He called UNITA leader Dr. Jonas Savimbi "an unhelpful player in the process in recent months."

Apparently fearing peace accords were unraveling, Annan recommended at least a six-week delay in further withdrawals of U.N. peacekeepers. He said 2,650 military personnel should stay until the end of October "given the precious situation in Angola," and the need to give the parties an additional chance to complete the peace process.

His report was to have triggered sanctions against UNITA, as threatened by the Security Council. But diplomats said the council, which will discuss Angola next Wednesday, would either delay sanctions for two weeks or impose them with a two-week grace period before they went into effect.
Envoys said since Annan wrote the report, Alione Blondin Beye, the U.N. special envoy in Angola, wanted to verify UNITA's latest proposals that touch on the council's demands.
The Angola government itself, they said, would rather call UNITA's bluff than have sanctions imposed immediately, which they believed were hard to enforce.

Possible sanctions could include a travel ban against UNITA leader Savimbi and other officials. Other measures, such as freezing UNITA bank accounts abroad, are being considered but might not be enacted until a later date because of the difficulty in carrying them out.

The council had imposed an arms embargo on UNITA but apparently Savimbi is able to keep supply lines open despite the fall of President Mobutu Sese Seko in the neighboring Democratic Republic of the Congo, formerly Zaire. Mobutu was one of UNITA's principal backers.

The council has demanded that UNITA demilitarize all its forces, transform its radio station into a non-partisan broadcasting facility and cooperate fully in extending government administration throughout the country as required in 1994 peace agreements signed in Lusaka, Zambia.

After two decades of civil war, UNITA, the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola, entered into a unity government in April with the MPLA, the Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola.

The conflict, after independence from Portugal in 1975, became a superpower proxy fight with the United States and the former white government of South Africa supporting Savimbi and the Soviet Union and Cuba supporting the now-ruling MPLA.

But UNITA still controls about 70 percent of the country, including Angola's diamond mines, and only a minority of its fighters have been demobilized and incorporated into a new national Angolan army.
Angolan government forces have escalated attacks against UNITA since the fall of Mobutu.
